Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'God is a Spirit' (pneuma ho theos) — Cyril reads this as ontological statement (the divine nature is spiritual, not material) and as missiological imperative (those who would worship a spiritual God must be spiritually transformed). Against the Anthropomorphites who attributed bodily form to God, Cyril insists the verse settles the question: God has no parts, no extension, no spatial location. Yet against any Hellenizing collapse of God into pure abstraction, Cyril preserves the personal-relational character: the Spirit-God is the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit — three Persons in one spiritual essence. Worship 'in spirit and in truth' is therefore the only worship corresponding to God's actual mode of being.

'My meat is to do the will of Him that sent me, and to finish His work' Cyril reads as Christ's self-disclosure of the perfect harmony between His human will and the Father's eternal will. Against the Apollinarian denial of Christ's human soul (or against any reading that would make Christ's will merely divine), Cyril here recognizes that Christ has a genuinely human will, but it is so perfectly conformed to the Father's will that 'doing the Father's will' becomes His characteristic sustenance — what physical food is to bodily life, the doing of the divine will is to Christ's incarnate human life. This is the seed of the dyothelite-anticipation that becomes explicit in later Greek theology, though Cyril himself does not yet use those terms.

The Samaritans' climactic confession — 'This is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world' (ho sōtēr tou kosmou) — Cyril emphasizes as the proleptic Gentile recognition of Christ's universal salvific scope. The Samaritans, themselves marginal to Jewish covenant identity, become the prototype for the Gentile inclusion that will mark the post-Pentecost Church. 'Saviour of the world' is for Cyril a title both universal (Christ saves the world, not merely a portion) and particular (each person is saved as individual within that universal scope). The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors Photine (the traditional name of the Samaritan woman) on the 26th of Hidar — her witness to her village becomes the first apostolic missionary act recorded in John.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's promise to the Samaritan woman — 'Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life' — Cyril reads pneumatologically: the water is the Holy Spirit Himself, given through Christ as His own gift to those who receive Him. The water's spring inside the believer (pēgē hydatos hallomenou) figures the Spirit's permanent indwelling, distinguished from the Old Covenant prophetic intermittent inspiration. 'Springing up' (hallomenou) carries the sense of leaping, dynamic ascent — the Spirit's indwelling is not static container but living source of theosis.

'The hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth' Cyril reads as the abrogation of the geographic-cultic restriction (Jerusalem temple / Mt. Gerizim) in favor of pneumatic-Christological worship. 'In spirit' is for Cyril 'in the Holy Spirit' (the worshipper's pneumatic transformation), and 'in truth' is 'in the Truth that is Christ' (Jn 14:6). True worship after the Incarnation is therefore Trinitarian: to the Father, in the Spirit, through the Truth-Son. This passage grounds the Tewahedo liturgical doctrine that the Anaphora's prayer is itself the Spirit's praying through the Church to the Father, mediated by the Christological elements.
